Whenever you have another incident to add, just let me know and I'll file it alongside this one. We can look for common patterns like settings, time of day, or how well you know the person.

Around March 20th I was on a video call with a client named Martin Chu and I kept calling him "Michael" — three times during the call. He never corrected me, which was almost worse because I only realized after I hung up and checked the email thread. I felt that low-grade cringe sitting in my stomach for the rest of the day.

Ouch, that sounds really uncomfortable — especially the delayed realization after the call. I've logged incident two: around March 20th, on a video call with client Martin Chu, you called him "Michael" three times. He didn't correct you; you only caught the error afterward by reviewing the email thread. The lingering embarrassment you describe is understandable. I'm already noticing a potential pattern: both Rebecca and Martin have names that share initial letters with the wrong name you used — R for Rachel/Rebecca, M for Michael/Martin. That same-first-letter confusion might be a consistent trigger for you.

Exactly, names starting with the same letter just blend together in my head, especially in group settings. One-on-one I'm usually fine but once there are more than four or five people I start swapping names. Anyway, third incident: I introduced my partner's friend as "Leah" when her actual name is Lena Vasquez at a dinner party last week. My partner nudged me under the table. Lena laughed it off though.

That's a helpful self-observation about group size being a trigger — it sounds like cognitive load from managing multiple social interactions causes the name-swapping. Incident three is logged: last week at a dinner party, you introduced your partner's friend as "Leah" when her name is Lena Vasquez. All three involve similar-sounding substitutions with matching first letters.

Yeah, I notice I'm less stressed about the casual ones. The dinner with Lena was relaxed, only six people, and she laughed it off. It's the professional settings that really get to me — like the Martin Chu call felt awful because it was a client interaction. My friend Dana says she does the same thing with her boss, calls him Greg when his name is Craig, but he apparently doesn't even notice.

That distinction between casual and professional settings makes a lot of sense. The stakes feel higher in work contexts, so the embarrassment amplifies. Dana's experience with Greg/Craig is interesting — it shows how common same-letter swaps are, and that some people genuinely don't register it. For your tracking purposes, I'll note that professional settings with higher social pressure seem to intensify both the frequency and the emotional impact of these mix-ups. We can use that insight when we build strategies later.
